content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the issue of requiring to access a complete and correct symbolic model when combining symbolic methods with reinforcement learning (RL). To address the issue, this work proposes a new method for learning optimistic symbolic approximations of the underlying model in an online fashion. Besides, theoretical results are provided to further analyze the proposed algorithm. Finally, experiments were conducted on three traditional planning domains (Blocks, Elevator, Gripper) and one traditional RL benchmark (Minigrid), with results demonstrating its effectiveness in terms of solvability, the average time, and the number of samples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Symbolic representation has been shown promising in guiding RL for the efficient exploration, explainability, and human-machine interaction. This is an interesting work targets to learning a symbolic representation for effective exploration within RL, particularly under the sparse reward setting. It would be intriguing to both the communities of symbolic planning and RL.


Weaknesses:
- The presentation of the paper could be improved. For example, how the symbolic model in this work is learned in an online fashion? As mentioned in the related work, I notice some of them allowing to learn the symbolic representation in an online setting, what's the difference between the proposed method and the existing work? How human guidance/ advice interact with this symbolic representation in practice? There lacks more technical details. For the pseudocode of algorithm 1, it would be more clear if the procedures, such as PruneModel, UpdateModel, can be referred to a more specific steps/ equations/ definitions. Besides, I am wondering how does this learned representation interact with RL since I didn't find too many details about this in the paper. Also, how does this learned representation help RL w.r.t. the effective exploration? Does it aim to reduce the exploration space by using prior knowledge or guide RL to explore more meaningful states?
- Current empirical results could not well support the claims on addressing the problem of effective exploration and speeding up the learning process with human minimal input. Comparing with Q-learning with the proposed method (w/wo lifting) in Table 1 looks unfair to me. For the planning domains, there should be included some planning baseline in addition to the proposed method. Particularly, I am quite curious why hierarchical RL fails in Minigrid domain? Even if hierarchical RL doesn't work, it at least has a better performance than flat Q-learning. Can you elaborate more on this?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6083 by Reviewer dzDP

content.title: Response to Reviewer dzDP
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. We updated our draft to reflect those comments. In particular, the discussion related to specific functions discussed in the pseudocode are included in Section 4.2 and the potential interaction with the Q learning algorithm is provided at the end of the same section. Below we have provided some responses to specific questions raised.

Interaction between these Models and RL Algorithm: We see the primary use of these methods to be as a way to initialize the Qvalue function estimates, which can then be improved by the RL algorithm over time. Additionally, after the initialization, we can also employ it during the learning process like a traditional exploration strategy (note that in these later deployments the model will start from a more informative estimate of the model). 

Other Online Model Learning Work: We only found two other online model learning works, namely [1] and [2] that tries to learn a complete planning model (we have included a discussion about this work in the new draft). Works like [3] only learn some components of the overall model and thus are not suitable for our purposes. The main difference between [1],[2] and our work is the underlying objective of the learning process. While the objective of that work (and in fact most of the other model learning work) is to accurately reconstruct the underlying model, ours is to merely retrieve a path to the goal. This is because we are employing it purely as a means of driving the exploration. This brings up new challenges and opportunities that are unique to our setting.  For example, we are unaware of any other methods that try to maintain an optimistic approximation of the underlying planning model. Additionally, it is worth noting that the problem of building a planning model to drive exploration, in itself involves balancing exploration and exploitation. After all, we would want to be cognizant of what actions we test as part of a potential plan to the goal (and how often we test them).

Symbolic Baseline: We have now included a symbolic baseline to the current set of experiments. As discussed in our response to reviewer DcWG, in the one problem the baseline method was able to handle, the baseline required almost 900 times more samples than out method.

Hierarchical RL: One of the specific advantages our method provides over traditional hierarchical RL methods is that our method allows us to perform goal directed exploration. While the abstractions provide some structure to the underlying problem, the meta-controller is still limited by the need to perform blind exploration using the temporal extended actions.

[1] Lamanna, Leonardo, et al. "Online Learning of Action Models for PDDL Planning." IJCAI. 2021.

[2] Jaime G Carbonell and Yolanda Gil. Learning by experimentation: The operator refinement method. In Machine learning, pp. 191–213. Elsevier, 1990.

[3] Sreedharan, Sarath, et al. "Bridging the Gap: Providing Post-Hoc Symbolic Explanations for Sequential Decision-Making Problems with Inscrutable Representations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.01080 (2020).

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6083 by Reviewer mjER

content.title: Response to mjER
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their constructive comments. We have tried to address the comments that the reviewer had raised about the clarity of the paper. 
One of the reviewer’s comments was not clear to us: “This paper also relies on human input and a goal directed planner, those two assumptions do not seem realistic to solve more general problems.”
We would appreciate it if the reviewer could clarify what assumptions about a goal-directed planner would be unrealistic. 
Below, we have tried to respond to some specific comments the reviewer had

Deterministic Domains: As pointed out in our response to reviewer DcWG, our method remains a viable technique in stochastic settings. Please see the answer to reviewer DcWG for additional details.
It is not clear that stochasticity is one of the main causes of difficulty of exploration in reinforcement learning in sparse reward domains. Evidently, the exploration remains hard even in the absence of stochasticity. One foundational problem here is large state spaces and lack of any guidance to drive the agent towards high reward states. In order to make the experimental setting clean, we have decided to focus on the deterministic environments.

Blocksworld: Apart from the historical importance of the problem, blockworld is one of the simplest problems that really showcase the combinatorial explosion that occurs when considering a relational or object oriented representation of the problem. In fact, for a relatively small number of blocks (just above 100), the state space is larger than chess or Go (3.86E+172 states for a problem with 104 blocks). It is also worth noting that optimal planning for blocksworld is an NP-Hard problem. The reviewer can refer to [2] for a more detailed discussion on the importance of the blocksworld as a useful benchmark for sequential decision-making problems. 

Assumption made about Human Input: Please note that use of human feedback is a common assumption made within many reinforcement learning methods that leverage human-feedback. However, we would argue that the assumptions made in this work are much more reasonable than the assumptions made by existing works in this direction. Most of the prominent works in this direction expects a human observer to watch the RL agent execution and then provide feedback with respect to the agent behavior (cf. [3] and [4]). We, on the other hand, are only asking the human to provide a list of objects that may be relevant to a given action (please see an example in the response to reviewer DcWG). 
Even in that case, our method allows the human to provide a superset of objects. In fact, for domains with a bounded number of objects we can in theory start with the set of all objects, not requiring explicit input from the human.

Non-Tabular Q learning: Given the sparse reward settings and the fact that the actor is restricted to starting episodes from a specific initial state, Q learning based methods, regardless of whether it is tabular or using some form of function approximation, will be limited by its inability to generate useful Q value estimates. Since one can’t build any useful Q value approximations until a goal state is reached, which constitutes the entirety of our exploration problem.


[1] Camacho, Eduardo F., and Carlos Bordons Alba. Model predictive control. Springer science & business media, 2013.

[2] Slaney, John, and Sylvie Thiébaux. "Blocks world revisited." Artificial Intelligence 125.1-2 (2001): 119-153.

[3] Christiano, Paul F., et al. "Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

[4] Warnell, Garrett, et al. "Deep tamer: Interactive agent shaping in high-dimensional state spaces." Proceedings of the AAAI conference on artificial intelligence. Vol. 32. No. 1. 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a new algorithm for integrating off-the-shelf automatic symbolic planners with online RL for efficient exploration in the sparse reward setting. The authors propose to itteratively refine a symbolic representation that a planner uses to predict paths towards a goal, which gets rolled out in the environment. It is theoretically proven that the proposed algorithm terminates, provided some conditions on the planner are satisfied. The authors show results comparing their method to Q-learning and show an improvement in the outlined domains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The paper presents the problem setting and background in a very rigorous manner, and the theoretical guarantees are relevant to the proposed task. The paper includes code for reproduction.

Weaknesses:

The paper is lacking in thorough experimentation and results discussion. Additionally, a major limitation comes from the constraint to deterministic MDPs (which the authors acknowledge). Additionally, the paper assumes human input for annotation of the actions, which begs the question why the baseline is a Q-learning model, as opposed to something that similarly uses human guidance, i.e. imitation learning. Additionally, the use of online RL, as opposed to the more prevalent offline RL setting within the symbolic representations, is not well justified. It would be good to compare against other existing symbolic planning methods as well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow and clearly written. The presented approach is novel although perhaps of limited practicality. The appendix contains sufficient implementation details for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is clear and well written with good theoretical justification, however it is questionable if the proposed approach could scale to more complex and realistic domains (such as the kitchen domain from Danfei Xu, Roberto Martín-Martín, De-An Huang, Yuke Zhu, Silvio Savarese, Li Fei-Fei, Regression Planning Networks). I would be willing to increase my score if more detailed experiments are provided.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6083 by Reviewer DcwG

content.title: Response to Reviewer DcwG
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. Below we have provided responses to some specific questions the reviewer had raised

Deterministic Settings: As discussed in the paper, our basic method is directly applicable in stochastic settings, by assuming that the learned model is a determinization of the underlying true stochastic problem. Thus we can still maintain a deterministic version of the task, which is easier to plan with and the action sequences generated that way can then be used to drive the exploration in the true model. Such a determinization of models is a common technique used to simplify planning in works from both the symbolic planning community (eg: [1]) and control-theoretic planning literature (certainty equivalence is a core concept within model-predictive controllers [2]). In fact, such model determinization can be thought of as another way we are creating optimistic estimates of the underlying model.

Online vs Offline Model Learning: One of the big reasons we chose to focus on the online settings, is because it allows the planning techniques to leverage an important factor that has fueled recent successes in RL, namely the availability of powerful simulators. The availability of such simulators combined with access to efficient diverse planners allows us to generate goal reaching traces with high confidence, even when our model may be a loose approximation of the true underlying model. 

Symbolic Baseline: We have now included a baseline (one presented in [3]) that uses traces generated through random walks from the model to learn the symbolic model (provided in A.4.1). We specifically tested on the blocksworld domain with a budget of 600000 samples, where we found that the method was only able to learn a model capable of generating a valid plan for the first problem instance and required on average 548287.8 (averaged across five runs). This is nearly 900 times larger than the sample count required by our method on the same problem.

Kitchen Domain: We have now included an experiment on the symbolic part of the kitchen domain (provided in A.4.2). Under this domain, each action corresponds to the achievement of one of the highlevel subgoals. The relation between the various subgoals were encoded as per the description provided by Xu et al. 2019. For the experiments, we used a symbolic simulator, but as discussed by Xu et al. 2019, we can use a motion level planner to test the executability of each of these actions. The lifted version of our method was able to identify a valid plan in 61.46 sec using 24727.2 time steps (averaged across five runs) and the non lifted version took 393.57 secs and used 140681 samples (again averaged across five runs).

Human Feedback: The input we request from the human is very limited: a list of possible objects that might be related to a given action. For example, in the case of the action for unstacking block1 from block2, all the human has to identify is that action will only involve the blocks block1 and block2. It is also worth mentioning that access to this information is a common assumption made across existing works for learning symbolic models. We are unaware of any current RL methods that learn from such sparse feedback, all of the ones we are aware of usually require more involved feedback (for example [4],[5],and [6]).

[1] Yoon, Sung Wook, Alan Fern, and Robert Givan. "FF-Replan: A Baseline for Probabilistic Planning." ICAPS. Vol. 7. 2007.

[2] Camacho, Eduardo F., and Carlos Bordons Alba. Model predictive control. Springer science & business media, 2013.

[3] Brendan Juba and Roni Stern. Learning probably approximately complete and safe action models for stochastic worlds. In Thirty-Sixth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, AAAI, pp. 9795– 9804. AAAI Press, 2022.

[4] Christiano, Paul F., et al. "Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

[5] Warnell, Garrett, et al. "Deep tamer: Interactive agent shaping in high-dimensional state spaces." Proceedings of the AAAI conference on artificial intelligence. Vol. 32. No. 1. 2018.

[6] Guan, Lin, Sarath Sreedharan, and Subbarao Kambhampati. "Leveraging Approximate Symbolic Models for Reinforcement Learning via Skill Diversity." arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.02886 (2022).

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper presents an idea for using symbolic model learning to aid in exploration to find an optimal plan in goal-directed sequential decision making. The idea is to start with an overcomplete/optimistic model estimate, and then to refine/prune it as experience is gathered. Results are presented in several classical planning domains (e.g. blocksworld) as well as symbolic forms of RL-focused domains (e.g. minigrid, kitchen), showing that the proposed method outperforms various RL methods (Q-learning, HRL) and a symbolic baseline. While the central idea behind the paper is quite interesting and worthy of attention, the paper in its current form is not ready for publication at ICLR. While I and the reviewers appreciated the addition of the kitchen experiments and symbolic baseline, there was agreement that (1) the paper was difficult to understand, and would not be replicable as written; (2) the Q-learning baseline was inappropriate as it is not a method for exploration---something like Go-Explore (Ecoffet et al. 2021) would be more appropriate; and (3) a central claim of the paper is that the method is applicable to RL, but the paper does not actually demonstrate this empirically (e.g. by training an RL agent on the data generated by the symbolic exploration). As such, I recommend rejection.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: While an interesting idea, the paper is not written clearly enough for the method to be useful to the community. It also has a number of other limitations, such as inappropriate baselines and unsupported claims.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting: I held an AC/reviewer meeting as the scores of the reviewers were split and the reviewers had not responded to the authors. However, in the meeting it became apparent that despite the author response, all reviewers (including those who had given a positive score) had reasonable concerns with the paper. The biggest concern was the clarity of the paper, as all of us had difficulty understanding exactly how the method worked; this concern, while raised by the reviewers in their reviews, was not adequately addressed by the authors in their response. Other concerns included the adequacy of the baselines (which was partially addressed by the authors by including some additional baselines, but not fully as some of the baselines included were still felt to be inappropriate) and the applicability to RL (which was  clarified by the authors in their response, but also made clear that the method is only in principle applicable to RL and has not been demonstrated empirically in the paper). My biggest concern is the clarity of the paper; if it is not clear what was actually done, then it is of limited value to the scientific community, and this (along with the other concerns) leads me to my decision to reject.
